title.source: Section check: Museums, heritage and connections
title.back: Section check: Museums, heritage and connections
title.note: The section's Indonesian title from course.json.

intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 16–20. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.
intro.back: 10 questions about Lessons 16–20. No need to hurry. You may look at the lessons again and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.source: Seeing the clay piece in a building would give it a different context. What is context?
questions.0.question.back: Seeing the clay piece inside a building would give it a different context. What is context?

questions.0.options.0.text.source: The material that an object is made of
questions.0.options.0.text.back: The material used to make an object

questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The clay is the material. Context is the things around an object that help explain it. Look back at Lesson 16.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The clay is the material. Context is the things around an object that help explain it. Look at Lesson 16 again.

questions.0.options.1.text.source: The person who gave it to a museum
questions.0.options.1.text.back: The person who gave it to a museum

questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A donor is one part of an object's history. Context is everything around it that helps explain it. Look back at Lesson 16.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. A donor is one part of an object's history. Context is everything around it that helps explain it. Look at Lesson 16 again.

questions.0.options.2.text.source: The things around it that explain it
questions.0.options.2.text.back: The things around it that explain it

questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Its place, light, labels and nearby works all change how we see an object.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. Place, light, labels and nearby works all change the way we see an object.

questions.1.question.source: A museum label names the donor who gave an object. What does the donor's name show?
questions.1.question.back: A museum label names the donor who gave an object. What does the donor's name show?

questions.1.options.0.text.source: One part of the object's history
questions.1.options.0.text.back: One part of the object's history

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A donor's name is one part of the object's provenance. Records can still have gaps.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. A donor's name is one part of the object's provenance. Records can still have gaps.

questions.1.options.1.text.source: Every owner back to the first maker
questions.1.options.1.text.back: Every owner back to its first maker

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. One name does not prove the whole chain of owners. Records may have gaps. Look back at Lesson 16.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. One name does not prove the whole chain of its owners. Records can have gaps. Look at Lesson 16 again.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: Who made the object a long time ago
questions.1.options.2.text.back: Who made the object long ago

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The donor gave the object to the museum. The makers of these two works are not recorded. Look back at Lesson 16.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The donor gave the object to the museum. The makers of these two works are not recorded. Look at Lesson 16 again.

questions.2.question.source: The mosque's walls are tangible heritage. What does tangible mean here?
questions.2.question.back: The mosque's walls are tangible cultural heritage. What does the word “tangible” mean in this term?
questions.2.question.note: “tangible heritage” is the official term “warisan budaya benda” (Lesson 17 and TERMS), so the question asks what the word “benda” means in that term. Check that this reads clearly to learners.

questions.2.options.0.text.source: Skills that people pass on to others
questions.2.options.0.text.back: Skills that people pass on to others

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Skills that people pass on are intangible heritage. Look back at Lesson 17.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Skills that people pass on are intangible cultural heritage. Look at Lesson 17 again.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.note: “intangible heritage” → “warisan budaya takbenda”, the official term.

questions.2.options.1.text.source: Things you can see and touch
questions.2.options.1.text.back: Things you can see and touch

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. The walls are real things you can touch. The skills of the builders are a different kind of heritage.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. The walls are real things you can touch. The builders' skills are a different kind of heritage.

questions.2.options.2.text.source: A report about repairs to a building
questions.2.options.2.text.back: A report about repairs to a building

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A report is a source about a building. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Look back at Lesson 17.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A report is a source about a building. Tangible cultural heritage is the building itself. Look at Lesson 17 again.

questions.3.question.source: Why does the Great Mosque of Djenné need people's work every year?
questions.3.question.back: Why does the Great Mosque of Djenné need people's work every year?

questions.3.options.0.text.source: It must be painted a new colour.
questions.3.options.0.text.back: The mosque must be painted a new colour.

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The mosque is made of earth. Every year, people put new mud plaster on it. Look back at Lesson 17.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The mosque is made of earth. Every year, people put new mud plaster on it. Look at Lesson 17 again.

questions.3.options.1.text.source: Its earth walls need new plaster.
questions.3.options.1.text.back: Its earth walls need new plaster.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Its sun-baked earth bricks are covered in mud plaster. People put on new plaster every year.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. Its sun-dried earth bricks are covered in mud plaster. People put on new plaster every year.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.note: “sun-baked earth bricks” → “Bata tanahnya yang dikeringkan di bawah matahari” (its earth bricks dried under the sun), Lesson 17's wording.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: It is built again from new each year.
questions.3.options.2.text.back: The mosque is rebuilt from the start every year.

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. The yearly work is new plaster. Look back at Lesson 17.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. The yearly work is putting on new plaster. Look at Lesson 17 again.

questions.4.question.source: The Vietnamese plate and the Chinese jug both have blue designs. Which claim would need more evidence?
questions.4.question.back: The Vietnamese plate and the Chinese jug both have blue decoration. Which claim would need more evidence?
questions.4.question.note: “blue designs” → “hiasan biru” (blue decoration). “jug” is “kendi”, as Lesson 18.

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Looking alike does not prove copying. We would need other evidence for that.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. Looking alike does not prove copying. We would need other evidence for that.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the blue designs in the photos. Copying is what would need more evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. You can see the blue decoration in the photos. It is copying that would need more evidence. Look at Lesson 18 again.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: Their shapes are not the same
questions.4.options.2.text.back: Their shapes are not the same

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the plate and the jug have different shapes. Copying would need more evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. You can see that the plate and the jug have different shapes. Copying would need more evidence. Look at Lesson 18 again.

questions.5.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. Ama is a potter in the made-up town of Sela. She sees a flower design on a bowl from far away. She uses it on her own plates. She adds local fruit to it and changes the shape to suit her buyers.
questions.5.stimulus.body.back: This is a made-up example. Ama is a potter in the made-up town of Sela. She sees a flower decoration on a bowl from a faraway place. She uses it on her own plates. She adds local fruits and changes its shape to suit her buyers.
questions.5.stimulus.body.note: “design” → “hiasan” (decoration) here and in the feedback, so it is not confused with the glossary word “motif”.

questions.5.question.source: Which word from Lesson 18 describes what Ama does?
questions.5.question.back: Which word from Lesson 18 describes what Ama does?

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Export means sending goods to another place to sell. Ama changes a design. Look back at Lesson 18.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Export means sending goods to another place to sell. Ama changes a decoration. Look at Lesson 18 again.

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Attribution means naming a work's maker, place or time from evidence. Look back at Lesson 18.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Attribution means naming the maker, place or time of a work based on evidence. Look at Lesson 18 again.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Ama changes an idea to fit a new setting and her own buyers. That is adaptation.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. Ama changes an idea to suit a new setting and her own buyers. That is adaptation.

questions.6.question.source: Posada's skeleton pictures used satire. What is satire?
questions.6.question.back: Posada's skeleton pictures used satire. What is satire?

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Paper with cut-out designs is papel picado. Look back at Lesson 19.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Paper with cut-out designs is papel picado. Look at Lesson 19 again.

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. An offering, or its altar, is an ofrenda. Look back at Lesson 19.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. An offering, or its altar, is an ofrenda. Look at Lesson 19 again.

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Satire uses humour to make fun of how people act, or of power.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. Satire uses humour to make fun of how people behave, or of power.

questions.7.question.source: In one region of Mexico, the festival is called Xantolo. What does this show?
questions.7.question.back: In one region of Mexico, this festival is called Xantolo. What does this show?

questions.7.options.0.text.source: One festival name holds many local forms.
questions.7.options.0.text.back: One festival name covers many local forms.

questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The clothes, music and roles are not the same in each group. One name holds many local stories.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. The clothes, music and roles are not the same in each group. One name covers many local stories.

questions.7.options.1.text.source: Every community celebrates in the same way.
questions.7.options.1.text.back: Every community celebrates it in the same way.

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Place, family and belief shape different forms. Xantolo is one example. Look back at Lesson 19.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Place, family and belief shape different forms. Xantolo is one example of this. Look at Lesson 19 again.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: The festival began with Posada's skeleton print.
questions.7.options.2.text.back: The festival began with Posada's skeleton print.

questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Posada did not invent the festival. It is much older than his print. Look back at Lesson 19.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Posada did not invent the festival. The festival is much older than his print. Look at Lesson 19 again.

questions.8.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. Rani wants to know how people look after an old earth building in the made-up town of Kesso. She has three sources. One is a photo of the outside. One is a report on its care, with a date. One is a postcard of it at sunset.
questions.8.stimulus.body.back: This is a made-up example. Rani wants to know how people look after an old earth building in the made-up town of Kesso. She has three sources. One is a photo of its outside. One is a report on its care, which is dated. One more is a postcard of the building at sunset.

questions.8.question.source: Which source best fits Rani's question?
questions.8.question.back: Which source best fits Rani's question?

questions.8.options.0.text.source: The photo of the building's outside
questions.8.options.0.text.back: The photo of the building's outside

questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A photo shows shape and material. It does not explain how the building is looked after. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. A photo shows shape and material. A photo does not explain how the building is looked after. Look at Lesson 20 again.

questions.8.options.1.text.source: The dated report on its care
questions.8.options.1.text.back: The dated report on its care

questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A report on its care explains how the building is looked after. Choose evidence that fits the question.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. A report on its care explains how the building is looked after. Choose evidence that fits the question.

questions.8.options.2.text.source: The postcard showing it at sunset
questions.8.options.2.text.back: The postcard of the building at sunset

questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A postcard shows a pretty view. It does not explain the care. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A postcard shows a beautiful view. A postcard does not explain its care. Look at Lesson 20 again.

questions.9.question.source: The record of the clay piece from Java does not name its building. What should a careful explanation do?
questions.9.question.back: The record of the clay piece from Java does not name the building it came from. What should a careful explanation do?
questions.9.question.note: “does not name its building” → “tidak menyebut bangunan asalnya” (does not name the building it came from).

questions.9.options.0.text.source: Leave the missing detail as a question
questions.9.options.0.text.back: Let the missing detail stay a question

questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The evidence does not settle this. So the missing detail can stay a question.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. The evidence does not settle this. So the missing detail can stay a question.

questions.9.options.1.text.source: Make up a likely name for the old temple
questions.9.options.1.text.back: Make up a likely name for that old temple

questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. An explanation should not use an invented temple name. Look back at Lesson 20.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. An explanation should not use a made-up temple name. Look at Lesson 20 again.

questions.9.options.2.text.source: Say that it must come from Borobudur
questions.9.options.2.text.back: Say that the object must be from Borobudur

questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The record does not prove that it came from Borobudur. Look back at Lessons 16 and 20.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The record does not prove that the object came from Borobudur. Look at Lessons 16 and 20 again.

results.high.source: Well done. You know a lot about how museums, care and traditions shape what a work means.
results.high.back: Very good. You know a lot about how museums, care and traditions shape the meaning of a work.

results.middle.source: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.
results.middle.back: Good work. You remember many main ideas. Look again at any lesson you want to check.

results.low.source: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 16–20, then try again whenever you like.
results.low.back: Thank you for trying. Look at Lessons 16–20 again, then try again whenever you want.
